topic_title: Christmas Paper Chain: 8 Ideas From Classic to Countdown
intro: A paper chain needs only strips, something to join them and time, which is why it works for classrooms, parties and an afternoon at the kitchen table. Three choices shape the result. Paper weight decides how long the chain lasts, since thin paper tears under its own weight on a long run. The fastener decides the pace: a stapler is quickest, glue sticks are safest for small hands, and tape sits in between. Strip size sets the look, with one inch by eight inches as the usual starting point. Plan on roughly six links for every foot of chain.

picks.breed: Classic Red and Green Loop Chain
picks.description: This is the version most people picture: alternating red and green loops made from one by eight inch strips of construction paper. It ranks first because every step is within reach of a four or five year old, and a pack of construction paper costs a few dollars and yields hundreds of links. Cut the strips with a paper trimmer or guillotine to keep them even, since wobbly scissor cuts are the main reason chains look untidy. Form the first loop, thread the next strip through it and close it, and repeat. Add white as a third color to make the pattern read as candy cane stripes. Construction paper fades in direct sun over a few weeks, so hang the chain away from a south-facing window if you want to keep it.
picks.best_for: Preschool and early elementary children, classrooms and large family groups
picks.skip_if: You want a chain that survives storage, because thin construction paper tears and fades quickly
picks.quirky_fact: A standard 9 by 12 inch sheet cut the short way gives twelve strips, enough for about two feet of chain.

picks.description: A countdown chain turns the craft into a daily ritual. Make 24 links for an Advent count from December 1, or one for each day left when you start, and number them so the last link to come off is Christmas Eve. One link is torn or cut away each morning, and the shrinking chain shows young children how long is left in a way a calendar does not. Writing something inside each strip before closing it adds a second layer: a film to watch, cookies to bake, a card to send. Use cardstock or heavier paper for this one, since it is handled daily. A paper star or bell shape at the top gives the chain a fixed point to hang from on a door or bedpost.
picks.best_for: Families with children who keep asking how many days are left
picks.skip_if: You are starting after mid-December, when a short chain has little impact
picks.quirky_fact: Because one link comes off each day, the chain should hang where a child can reach the bottom link without a chair.

picks.description: Brown kraft paper gives the chain a plain, natural look that sits well with dried orange slices, pine and wooden ornaments. Cut strips from a roll of kraft wrapping paper or from paper grocery bags, which makes this the lowest-cost option if you already have bags at home. Kraft paper is stiffer than construction paper, so loops hold a rounder shape and the chain lasts the season. Staples disappear against the brown better than tape. To finish the look, tie short lengths of jute or red and white baker's twine around every third or fourth link, or stamp the strips with a white ink pad before assembling. A single long run suits a mantel or stair rail better than a tree, where the brown can get lost against the branches.
picks.best_for: Farmhouse, Scandinavian and natural-toned Christmas rooms
picks.skip_if: You want bright traditional color, since an all-brown chain looks muted from across a room
picks.quirky_fact: Kraft paper takes its name from the German word for strength, which fits how well it holds a loop.

picks.description: Wrapping paper offcuts are too small to wrap anything but exactly the right size for chain strips, so this version costs nothing extra and uses paper that would otherwise be thrown out. Mix three or four patterns that share a color so the chain looks planned. Gift wrap is thinner than construction paper and often printed on one side only, so fold each strip in half lengthwise with the pattern facing out before looping it. That doubles the thickness and hides the white back. Glue stick slides on glossy or foil wrap, so use a stapler or double-sided tape. The finished chain matches the presents under the tree, which is a pleasing detail on a mantel or along a gift table at a party.
picks.best_for: Using up scraps after an evening of wrapping presents
picks.skip_if: Your gift wrap is very thin or plasticky foil, which creases and splits at the fold
picks.quirky_fact: Wrapping paper with glitter or a foil coating is often not accepted in household paper recycling, so reusing scraps keeps some out of the bin.

picks.description: Scrapbook paper printed on both sides solves the main weakness of patterned chains, the blank white inside of each loop. Holiday paper pads usually hold 12 by 12 inch sheets in coordinated plaids, stripes and small prints, and one pad is enough for a long chain with paper left over for gift tags. The stock is heavier than construction paper, close to light cardstock, so the links stay crisp and the chain stores flat for another year. Cut strips one inch by six inches for a neat, compact chain, or a full twelve inches for large loops across a window. A stapler copes best with the thickness. It costs more per link than any paper option above, which is why it sits in the middle of the list.
picks.best_for: Adults and older children who want a polished, reusable chain
picks.skip_if: You are supplying a whole class or party, where pad paper becomes expensive fast
picks.quirky_fact: The 12 by 12 inch scrapbook sheet matches the page size of the standard scrapbook album.

picks.description: Instead of loops, this chain links cut snowflakes edge to edge. Fold a square of thin white paper into a triangle three times, snip notches along the folds and open it out, then join the flakes at their tips with a small staple or a dot of glue. Lightweight printer paper or round coffee filters cut far more easily than cardstock through six or eight layers. Vary the flake sizes between four and eight inches for a natural look. Strung across a window, the chain throws patterned shadows in low winter sun. It takes much longer per foot than loops and the delicate tips tear easily, so treat it as a slower project for one window or a mirror instead of a whole room.
picks.best_for: Windows and children old enough to use scissors with confidence
picks.skip_if: You need many feet of chain quickly, because each flake takes several minutes
picks.quirky_fact: Folding the paper into six sections instead of eight gives a six-pointed flake, the same symmetry real snow crystals have.
picks.product_name: White Round Coffee Filters Basket Style

picks.description: A star garland swaps loops for flat or folded stars threaded on string. The quickest method uses a star paper punch of two to three inches on cardstock, then a sewing machine or needle and thread run through the center of each star with a small gap between them. Punching is fast, and a single sheet gives a dozen or more stars. For a fuller look, glue two stars back to back over the thread and bend the points slightly. Gold, cream and kraft brown look calm together; red and white is brighter. Because the stars spin freely on the thread, the garland moves in any draft, so it works best hung vertically in a window or down a wall instead of swagged across a tree.
picks.best_for: A quieter, more grown-up alternative to loop chains
picks.skip_if: You have no paper punch and do not want to cut dozens of stars by hand
picks.quirky_fact: Hung vertically with a bead or small weight at the bottom, star garlands tangle far less than when draped side to side.

picks.description: Felt copies the look of a paper chain in a material that can be packed away and reused for years. Cut craft felt sheets into strips one inch by seven inches with a rotary cutter and ruler, then close each loop with a stapler, a dab of hot glue or a few stitches. Felt is soft, so the loops flatten a little under their own weight and the chain drapes more than a paper one, which suits a tree or bed frame. It is safe around toddlers and pets in the sense that it will not tear into small soggy pieces when grabbed. The trade-offs are cost and effort: felt costs several times more than paper per link, and cutting it cleanly takes sharp tools, so it ranks last for a quick craft.
picks.best_for: Anyone who wants to make one chain and reuse it every year
picks.skip_if: You want a quick, cheap activity for young children to do themselves
picks.quirky_fact: Most craft felt sheets are made from acrylic or recycled polyester fibers, not wool, which keeps the price low.

faqs.question: What size should paper chain strips be?
faqs.answer: One inch wide by eight to nine inches long is the common size, and it is easy to cut from letter-size paper or 9 by 12 inch construction paper. Wider strips of one and a half to two inches look bolder on a mantel or doorway. Shorter strips of about five inches make small loops that suit a tabletop tree. Keep all strips the same length so the chain hangs evenly.

faqs.question: How many strips do I need for a paper chain?
faqs.answer: With one by eight inch strips, each link adds about two inches of length once it overlaps and interlocks, so count on roughly six links per foot. A six-foot mantel takes about 36 to 40 strips, and a chain that wraps a six-foot tree several times can need 150 or more. One 9 by 12 inch sheet gives twelve one-inch strips.

faqs.question: Is glue, tape or a stapler best for paper chains?
faqs.answer: A stapler is fastest and holds for the whole season, so it suits older children and adults making long chains. Glue sticks are safest for preschoolers but need each link held for several seconds, and the bond can fail on glossy paper. Double-sided tape or clear tape is a good middle option. For glittered or foil paper, use staples or tape, because glue stick does not grip the coating well.

faqs.question: How do I make a Christmas countdown paper chain?
faqs.answer: Cut one strip for each day you want to count, usually 24 or 25, and write a number on each before joining them in order. Hang the chain with the highest number at the bottom and remove one link each day so it gets shorter as Christmas approaches. Many families write a small activity or a kind act on the inside of each strip.

faqs.question: How do I store paper chains so they last until next year?
faqs.answer: Paper chains crush easily, so lay them loosely in a wide, shallow box with tissue between layers instead of stuffing them into a bag. Keep the box somewhere dry, since damp makes construction paper fade and warp. Chains made from cardstock or felt survive storage best. Thin construction paper chains are often easier to recycle and remake.

seo_title: Christmas Paper Chain: 8 Easy Ideas for 2026
answer: The classic red and green loop chain is the best place to start, followed by a numbered countdown chain and a kraft paper version with twine. The deciding factor is who is making it: plain loops suit young children and big groups, while snowflake and star chains need scissors skills and more patience.
method: Picked from Pinterest's trending searches for Christmas paper chains, then ordered by how easy each version is for children to make, what the supplies cost and how well the finished chain holds up through December.
